verdicts.quote: “Most of the time, OAuth is the preferred method of authentication for developers, users, and Asana as a platform.”
verdicts.reason: Asana supports PATs, but its docs explicitly prefer OAuth for apps that act on users’ accounts, which is what a multi-tenant agent toolkit would use.

verdicts.quote: “Submitting your app for review is not required to obtain a token. You only need to submit your app if you intend to: Make your app available to users in any Asana workspace, beyond your own organization or development environment; [or] List your app publicly on the Asana app directory.”
verdicts.reason: Credentials are self‑serve, but distribution beyond your own org or a public listing requires Asana’s review, matching “app_review.”

verdicts.quote: “The Asana API is a RESTful interface, providing programmatic access to much of the data in the system… [and has] a comprehensive reference for objects, schemas, and endpoints available in the API.”
verdicts.reason: Docs indicate wide coverage across many resources (tasks, projects, users, teams, portfolios, goals, webhooks, etc.), so breadth is broad.

verdicts.quote: “Asana’s official MCP server lets you interact with your Asana workspace through natural language—create tasks, search projects, analyze workload, and more…”
verdicts.reason: Asana publishes and maintains its own MCP server; this is not a community server.

verdicts.quote: “Submitting your app for review is not required to obtain a token. You only need to submit your app if you intend to: Make your app available to users in any Asana workspace, beyond your own organization…”
verdicts.reason: The API and MCP server are documented and creds are self‑serve (buildable now), but real distribution requires app review; plus standard API rate limits and some enterprise‑gated endpoints add constraints.
